posts:
Three of the biggest security incidents of the last three weeks: Binance (29 Oct), Keplr's Google/Apple-login wallets via their provider Web3Auth, and the Across domain hijack (10 Nov).

On what's been disclosed, none of them broke the cryptography.

Binance: a compromised engineer's laptop may have given access to a service container (its preliminary finding).

Keplr: the incident originated at Web3Auth, the provider behind its social-login wallets.

Across: social engineering at its registrar gave an attacker the domain.

All three went in through something around the keys, not the lock.

In the Keplr incident, wallets set up with a recovery phrase or hardware wallet weren't affected. Same app, different answer to 'who can reconstruct the key?'

So the useful question about any wallet isn't 'is it secure?'

It's: what can cause it to sign, who can change where you're sent, and can you leave?

We wrote up what happened, six questions to ask any wallet, what Swop has shipped against them, and what we haven't done (no third-party audit to date; wallets run on Privy today).

https://www.swopme.co/blog/crypto-hacks-2026-what-they-share
